units.title: Introduction to AI and Search
units.summary: Search algorithms explore states to reach a goal. Breadth-first search finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. A* uses a heuristic to guide the search, and an admissible heuristic never overestimates the true cost.

questions.text: Which search uses a FIFO queue and finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
questions.explanation: BFS expands level by level, so the first path it finds has the fewest edges.

questions.text: What makes A* different from uniform cost search?
options: It adds a heuristic estimate of the remaining cost
questions.explanation: A* ranks nodes by cost so far plus an estimate of the cost to the goal.

questions.text: A heuristic is admissible when it:
options: Overestimates the cost to the goal
questions.explanation: Admissibility guarantees that A* with this heuristic returns an optimal path.

units.title: Machine Learning Basics
units.summary: Supervised learning uses labeled data to predict outputs. Regression predicts continuous values and classification predicts categories. Overfitting means a model memorizes training data and generalizes poorly.

questions.text: Supervised learning requires:
questions.explanation: Supervised learning learns a mapping from inputs to known labels.

questions.text: Overfitting means the model:
options: Fits training data but generalizes poorly
questions.explanation: It captures noise in the training set, so accuracy on new data drops.

questions.text: Which is a regression task?
questions.explanation: Regression predicts a continuous number, such as a price.

units.title: Neural Networks and Activation Functions
units.summary: A neural network stacks layers of weighted sums followed by activation functions. Activations add non-linearity, which lets the network learn complex patterns. ReLU outputs max(0, x), and softmax turns output scores into class probabilities.

questions.text: The main purpose of an activation function is to:
questions.explanation: Without non-linearity, stacked layers collapse into one linear function.

questions.text: ReLU outputs:
questions.explanation: ReLU passes positive values unchanged and sets negative values to zero.

questions.text: Softmax is commonly used in the output layer for:
questions.explanation: Softmax produces values between 0 and 1 that sum to 1 across classes.

units.title: Backpropagation and Gradient Descent
units.summary: Backpropagation computes gradients of the loss with respect to each weight using the chain rule. Gradient descent updates weights by moving against the gradient. The learning rate controls the step size.

questions.text: Backpropagation computes gradients using which rule?
questions.explanation: The chain rule propagates derivatives backward through each layer.

questions.text: A learning rate that is too large usually causes:
questions.explanation: Steps overshoot the minimum, so the loss can bounce or grow.

questions.text: Gradient descent updates parameters by moving:
questions.explanation: The negative gradient points in the direction that reduces the loss.

units.title: Convolutional Neural Networks
units.summary: CNNs use convolution kernels that slide over an image and share weights across positions. Pooling layers reduce spatial size. CNNs suit grid-like data such as images.

questions.text: Convolution kernels in a CNN share:
questions.explanation: Weight sharing lets one kernel detect the same pattern anywhere in the image.

questions.text: Max pooling:
options: Downsamples by keeping the maximum in each window
questions.explanation: Pooling keeps the strongest response in each window and reduces size.

questions.text: CNNs are especially well suited for:
questions.explanation: Local spatial structure in grids is what convolutions exploit.

units.title: Introduction to OS and System Calls
units.summary: An operating system manages hardware and provides services to programs. System calls are the interface through which programs request services. The CPU runs in user mode or kernel mode, and only kernel mode can run privileged instructions.

questions.text: A system call is:
options: An interface for programs to request OS services
questions.explanation: Programs use system calls such as read, write and fork to ask the kernel for work.

questions.text: Which mode has full access to hardware?
questions.explanation: Kernel mode can run privileged instructions and access all hardware.

questions.text: Which is NOT a core OS function?
options: Compiling source code into machine code
questions.explanation: Compiling is the job of a compiler, not the operating system.

units.title: Process Scheduling
units.summary: The scheduler chooses which ready process runs next. FCFS is simple but can cause the convoy effect. SJF gives the minimum average waiting time when non-preemptive. Round Robin gives each process a fixed time quantum.

questions.text: FCFS scheduling can suffer from:
questions.explanation: A long job at the front makes short jobs wait behind it.

questions.text: Non-preemptive SJF minimizes:
questions.explanation: Running shorter jobs first reduces the average wait across all jobs.

questions.text: Round Robin performance depends mainly on:
questions.explanation: A very large quantum behaves like FCFS, and a very small one adds overhead.

units.title: Process Synchronization
units.summary: When threads share data, unsynchronized access causes race conditions. Mutexes and semaphores enforce mutual exclusion. A binary semaphore behaves like a lock.

questions.text: A mutex is used to:
questions.explanation: Only one thread at a time may hold the lock on a shared resource.

questions.text: A semaphore initialized to 1 acts as:
options: A binary semaphore like a lock
questions.explanation: With a count of 1, the semaphore allows only one holder at a time.

questions.text: A race condition occurs when:
options: Threads access shared data concurrently without synchronization
questions.explanation: The final result depends on the timing of the threads.

units.title: Deadlocks
units.summary: Deadlock needs four conditions at once: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. The Banker algorithm avoids deadlock by checking that the system stays in a safe state. Ordering resource requests breaks circular wait.

questions.text: The four necessary conditions for deadlock include:
options: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait
questions.explanation: All four must hold at the same time for a deadlock to occur.

questions.text: The Banker algorithm:
options: Avoids deadlock by checking for a safe state
Only detects deadlock after it happens
questions.explanation: A request is granted only if the system can still finish all processes.

questions.text: Breaking circular wait is done by:
questions.explanation: If every process requests resources in the same order, no cycle can form.

units.title: Memory Management
units.summary: Paging divides logical memory into fixed-size pages mapped to physical frames. A page fault happens when the needed page is not in physical memory. Segmentation divides memory into variable-size logical segments.

questions.text: Paging divides:
questions.explanation: Pages map to physical frames of the same size.

questions.text: A page fault means:
options: The requested page is not in physical memory
questions.explanation: The OS loads the page from disk, then the instruction resumes.

questions.text: Segmentation divides memory into:
questions.explanation: Segments follow the logical structure of a program, such as code and stack.

units.title: Asymptotic Analysis
units.summary: Big-O notation gives an upper bound on how running time grows with input size. Binary search runs in O(log n). Growth rates order from O(log n) and O(n) up to O(n log n) and O(n squared).

questions.text: Big-O describes:
options: An upper bound on growth rate
questions.explanation: Big-O ignores constants and machine speed and focuses on growth.

questions.text: The time complexity of binary search is:
questions.explanation: Each step halves the remaining search space.

questions.text: Which grows fastest?
questions.explanation: Quadratic growth outpaces linearithmic, linear, and logarithmic growth.

units.title: Divide and Conquer
units.summary: Divide and conquer splits a problem, solves the parts, and combines the results. Merge sort follows the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), giving O(n log n). Quick sort degrades to O(n squared) when pivots are always the smallest or largest element.

questions.text: Merge sort follows the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). Its complexity is:
questions.explanation: The recursion depth is log n and each level does O(n) work.

questions.text: The three steps of divide and conquer are:
questions.explanation: Split the problem, solve subproblems, then merge their answers.

questions.text: Quick sort reaches its worst case when:
options: The pivot is always the smallest or largest
questions.explanation: Partitions become unbalanced, so the recursion depth grows to n.

units.title: Greedy Algorithms
units.summary: Greedy algorithms make the locally best choice at each step. They are optimal when the problem has the greedy choice property and optimal substructure. Activity selection picks the earliest finishing activity, and Huffman coding merges the two lowest-frequency nodes.

questions.text: A greedy algorithm is correct when the problem has:
options: Greedy choice property and optimal substructure
questions.explanation: These two properties guarantee that local choices lead to a global optimum.

questions.text: Activity selection chooses:
questions.explanation: Finishing early leaves the most room for the remaining activities.

questions.text: Huffman coding builds its tree by repeatedly merging:
questions.explanation: Rare symbols get longer codes and frequent symbols get shorter ones.

units.title: Dynamic Programming
units.summary: Dynamic programming applies when a problem has overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure. Memoization caches subproblem results. The 0/1 knapsack table has n times W entries.

questions.text: Dynamic programming applies when a problem has:
questions.explanation: Caching overlapping subproblems avoids repeated work.

questions.text: The 0/1 knapsack DP table typically has size:
questions.explanation: One row per item and one column per capacity from 0 to W.

questions.text: Memoization means:
questions.explanation: Each subproblem is computed once and its result is stored for reuse.

units.title: Graph Algorithms
units.summary: Dijkstra finds shortest paths when edge weights are non-negative. Kruskal builds a minimum spanning tree by sorting edges and using union-find. Topological sort orders the vertices of a directed acyclic graph.

questions.text: Dijkstra requires:
questions.explanation: Negative edges can break the greedy assumption that finalized distances stay final.

questions.text: Kruskal algorithm uses:
questions.explanation: Edges are added in increasing weight unless they form a cycle.

questions.text: Topological sort applies to:
questions.explanation: A cycle would make a valid ordering impossible.
